A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same OKB research work. Their main text, equations, experimental figures, proofs and appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison, including the additional appendices and checklist in v2.

before.justification: V1 reports original reinforcement-learning experiments on Minecart, Highway, FetchPickAndPlace and Item Collection, including learning curves and a qualitative policy analysis in Figures 2–5.

after.justification: V2 retains these original experiments and policy analyses in Section 5 and Figures 2–5.

M1.justification: Appendix B adds an explicit input adaptation for signed linear rewards: augment features with their negatives, split positive and negative weight components, and normalize the resulting nonnegative weights. The core OKB, OK-LS and TrainOK algorithms remain unchanged; the existing experiments are not reported as using this adaptation.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same four domains, including FetchPickAndPlace with 2, 4, 6 and 8 reward features and the sequential nonlinear Item Collection task. The new theoretical treatment of signed rewards introduces no evaluated task coverage.

E2.justification: Figures 2–3 retain SFOLS and OKB-Uniform as comparators. Figure 4 retains SIP, DQN and the same three fixed-weight GPI policies. The new related-work citation is not an evaluated baseline.

E3.justification: V1 Appendix E states that architectures and hyperparameters were shared across methods; v2 Appendix F instead reports independently optimizing method-specific settings through grid search. This changes the reported comparison protocol without establishing that experiments were rerun. Interaction budgets, task generation, metrics and domain settings otherwise remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The uniform-task-selection ablation, reward-feature dimensionality sweep, nonlinear-transfer evaluation and Highway behavior trace are retained. V2 adds no empirical robustness, sensitivity or error analysis.

E5.justification: Both versions report 95% bootstrapped confidence intervals over 15 random seeds. V2's checklist repeats this information; it introduces no additional runs, uncertainty procedure or significance test.

E6.justification: The curves, confidence bands and policy trace in Figures 2–5 are unchanged. Appendix F newly reports approximate per-run durations: 2.5 hours for Item Collection, 6 for Minecart, 10 for FetchPickAndPlace and 25 for Highway. These are added runtime figures, not task-performance improvements.

T1.justification: V2 adds Appendix A.5's set-cover formulation and claimed conditions for a strictly smaller behavior basis, plus Appendix B's derivation reducing signed linear rewards to convex combinations over doubled features. These substantially expand the theoretical treatment. The existing proofs and nonlinear counterexample are retained; v1 Theorem 4.5 becomes v2 Proposition 4.4 without changing its substance.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central claims: constructing an optimal OK behavior basis, reducing the policies needed relative to a CCS, supporting certain nonlinear tasks, and outperforming GPI-based approaches increasingly as reward dimensionality grows.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations of the optimality check as primarily reducing training effort, explains the computational motivation for USFAs, and links smaller bases to shared sub-behaviors in compositional transfer. The existing empirical interpretations and nonlinear expressiveness limitations remain.

D1.justification: Appendix F adds NVIDIA A100-PCIE-40GB hardware, 32 GB RAM, approximate execution times and the grid-search description. The new checklist states that reproduction code is in supplementary material, while the appendix retains the promise of public release upon acceptance. The supplied PDFs establish these disclosures, not actual code availability.

R1.justification: Section 6 adds Kuric et al. (2024), positioning planning for tasks defined by finite-state automata as complementary work. The broader research positioning remains stable. Kim et al.'s change from 2024 to 2022 corrects metadata for the same cited work.

P1.justification: V2 makes localized prose revisions, reorders theoretical exposition, expands explanations and future-work discussion, and adds acknowledgments and a NeurIPS checklist. The seven main sections and overall narrative remain intact.

P2.justification: The main presentation is substantially rearranged: Algorithms 1–2 share a narrow column beside explanatory prose, Figure 1 becomes an inline display, Figure 2's panels are stacked, and Figures 4–5 are reduced and placed side by side. Algorithm styling and captions also change, while the underlying content of all six figures is retained.

improvement.justification: The signed-reward reduction and compute disclosures address gaps in v1. However, the new Appendix A.5 overstates its set-cover argument: sharing some sub-behaviors does not ensure a smaller cover, since each policy can still contain an indispensable unique behavior. Thus useful theoretical and reproducibility additions coexist with an unsupported new guarantee. With the experimental evidence unchanged, the net quality direction is uncertain.
